mainTopic: Stories of רבי יהושע בן חנניה and the קיסר, רב יהודה's teachings about bulls and אדם הראשון's bull, and creation made complete
overview: The amud opens with stories of רבי יהושע בן חנניה answering the Roman קיסר and his daughter. The קיסר cannot look at the sun, so he certainly cannot see the שכינה. His feast for God is swept away by wind and rain, which are only God's 'cleaning staff.' The קיסר's daughter mocks God as a carpenter and asks for a distaff. She is struck with צרעת and receives the distaff Rome gave every leper, and God does not take it back. The גמרא then brings teachings of רב יהודה about bulls: what a normal bull looks like, and how the bull of אדם הראשון had one horn and had its horns appear before its hooves. This supports רבי יהושע בן לוי, who says all of creation was made fully grown, with full understanding. רבי חנינא בר פפא adds that the grasses reasoned on their own to grow by their kinds, and the angel of the world praised ה׳. The amud ends as רבינא begins a question about grafting two grasses together, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The emperor cannot even look at the sun
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר asks to see God. רבי יהושע has him look at the summer sun, and he cannot. רבי יהושע argues: if you cannot look at one of God's servants, you certainly cannot look at the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said: I want to see Him. רבי יהושע stood him facing the sun in the summer and said: Look at it. He said: I can't. רבי יהושע said: The sun is just one of the servants standing before God, and you can't look at it. All the more so you can't look at the Divine Presence!
steps.whatsHappening: This story began just before our text: the קיסר said he wants to see God. Here רבי יהושע answers him with a live demonstration using the sun.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע does not argue in the abstract. He makes the קיסר feel his own limits. The argument is a קל וחומר: a servant of God is too bright to look at, so God Himself is surely beyond human sight.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so (a reasoning from smaller to greater)
The summer season, when the sun is strongest

phrases.english: I want to see Him.
He went and stood him facing the sun
in the season of Tammuz.
phrases.notes: That means the height of summer, when the sun is at its strongest.

phrases.english: He said to him: Look at it.
He said to him: I cannot.
He said to him: The sun,

phrases.aramaic: דְּחַד מִשַּׁמָּשֵׁי דְּקָיְימִי קַמֵּי דְּקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא
phrases.english: which is one of the servants that stand before the Holy One, Blessed be He,
you say: I cannot look at it.
The Divine Presence, is it not all the more so?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַל אוֹקְמֵיהּ לַהֲדֵי יוֹמָא בִּתְקוּפַת תַּמּוּז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the emperor's request to see God, which began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person cannot look at the sun, which is only God's servant, so he surely cannot see the שכינה.

steps.title: The emperor wants to make a feast for God
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר wants to prepare a meal for God. רבי יהושע warns that God's hosts are too many. When the emperor insists, he tells him to set it up on the wide seashore.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: I want to prepare a meal for your God. He said: You can't. Why not? Because His hosts are too many. The emperor said: Truly, I want to. רבי יהושע said: Then go prepare it on the shore of the great sea, where there is plenty of room.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. The קיסר makes a request, and רבי יהושע sets him up for the test that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע warns him first: God's 'army' of servants is too big to feed. The emperor will not back down, so רבי יהושע sends him to the biggest open space available. That sets up the lesson that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: His hosts, His armies of servants
The shore of the great sea

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה:
phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya:
I want to prepare bread for your God.
phrases.notes: "Bread" here means a full meal, a banquet.

phrases.english: He said to him: You cannot.
Why? His hosts are too many.
He said to him: Truly, I want to.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: פּוֹק צְבֵית לְגֻידָּא דִּרְבִיתָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: Go out and prepare it on the shore of the great sea,
where there is wide open space.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה: בָּעֵינָא דְּאִיצְבֵּית לֵיהּ נַהֲמָא לֵאלָהַיְכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about the same two people, on a similar theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The emperor insists on feasting God, and רבי יהושע sends him to the seashore to try.

steps.title: Wind and rain sweep away the feast
steps.stepSummary: Both of the emperor's attempts are swept into the sea. רבי יהושע explains that these were only God's sweepers and washers, and the emperor admits he cannot do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He worked six summer months, and a wind came and swept it all into the sea. He worked six winter months, and rain came and sank it all in the sea. He asked: What is this? רבי יהושע said: These are just the sweepers and floor-washers who go before Him. The emperor said: If so, I cannot do it.
steps.whatsHappening: The test from the last step plays out. The emperor fails twice and gives up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wind and rain, which are only God's lowliest 'cleaning staff', eat up a whole year's work. If the cleaners alone use up everything, the emperor could never feed God's full host. The emperor ends by admitting the point himself.
steps.whatToRemember: In both stories רבי יהושע uses the same move. A small part of God's creation (the sun, the wind and rain) is already too much for a human, so God Himself is far beyond us.

phrases.english: He worked the six months of summer,
a wind came and swept it into the sea.
He worked the six months of winter,
rain came and sank it in the sea.
He said to him: What is this?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנֵי כָּנוֹשָׁאֵי זָלוֹחָאֵי דְּאָתוּ קַמֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: These are the sweepers and washers who go before Him.
phrases.notes: He means the wind is the sweeper and the rain is the washer.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי הָכִי לָא מָצֵינָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: If so, I cannot.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי הָכִי לָא מָצֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the test set up in step 2 and gives its outcome.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even God's lowliest servants use up everything a human can offer, so no human can host God.

steps.title: The emperor's daughter mocks God as a carpenter
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר's daughter quotes a פסוק about God laying beams, calls God a 'carpenter', and asks mockingly that He make her a distaff.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor's daughter said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: Your God is a carpenter, as it is written: 'Who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters.' Tell Him to make me a distaff.
steps.whatsHappening: A third story begins. The daughter uses a פסוק to mock God, and this sets up רבי יהושע's response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She reads the word הַמְקָרֶה ('lays beams') very literally, as if God were a woodworker. Then she makes fun of Him by asking for a cheap little spinning tool.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters' (תהלים 104:3)
A distaff, a simple stick used for spinning wool

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ בַּת קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה:
phrases.english: The emperor's daughter said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya:
Your God is a carpenter,
as it is written: "Who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters."

phrases.aramaic: אֵימָא לֵיהּ דְּנֶעְבֵּיד לִי חֲדָא מַסְתּוּרִיתָא.
phrases.english: Tell Him to make me a distaff.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֱלָהֵיכוֹן נַגָּרָא הוּא, דִּכְתִיב הַמְקָרֶה בַמַּיִם עֲלִיּוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story with a different challenger.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: She reads a פסוק literally to shrink God down to a craftsman and dares Him to make a trivial tool.

steps.title: She is struck with צרעת and receives a distaff
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע agrees and prays. She is struck with צרעת and placed in the Roman market, where lepers were given a distaff. So she gets her distaff.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Very well. He prayed for her and she was struck with leprosy. They sat her in the market of Rome and gave her a distaff. It was the custom in Rome to give a distaff to every leper, who would sit in the market and untangle wool, so that people would see him and pray for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the daughter's mockery, and she receives her 'distaff' in a way she never expected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her request is fulfilled, but as a punishment. The Roman custom of giving lepers a distaff explains how she ended up holding one. God did 'make her a distaff', though not the way she meant.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not misread 'he prayed for mercy for her' as a prayer to help her. The outcome shows the prayer led to her being stricken, which is how she got the distaff.

phrases.english: He said: Very well,
he prayed for mercy for her and she was stricken with leprosy.
They sat her in the market of Rome
and they gave her a distaff,
since it was their custom that anyone stricken with leprosy in Rome
would be given a distaff,
and he would sit in the market and untangle bunches of wool,
so that people would see him
and pray for mercy on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: לְחַיֵּי, בְּעָא רַחֲמֵי עֲלַהּ וְאִינַּגְעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the daughter's mocking request in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Her mocking request is fulfilled as a punishment: she becomes a leper and is given a distaff, following the Roman custom.

steps.title: The daughter sits with her distaff, and God does not take back
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע passes the leprous daughter in the Roman market and asks if she likes the distaff God gave her. She asks him to tell God to take it back. He answers that our God gives but does not take back.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day רבי יהושע passed by and saw her sitting in the Roman market, untangling wool. He said: 'Do you like the distaff my God gave you?' She said: 'Tell your God to take back what He gave me.' He said: 'Our God gives. He does not take back.'
steps.whatsHappening: This closes the story of the קיסר's daughter. Her mocking request from earlier has come true, and רבי יהושע has the last word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier she mockingly asked God to 'make her a distaff.' Now she has one, but only because she is a leper. When she begs for God to remove it, רבי יהושע answers that what God gives, He does not take back. Her mockery turned back on her.

keyTerms.meaning: The Roman market, where the lepers sat
A distaff, the stick that holds wool for spinning
He gives, but He does not take back

steps.whatToRemember: The story ends with the daughter's mockery turned against her. She asked for a distaff and got one, through צרעת, and God does not take back what He gives.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא חָלֵיף הָתָם,
phrases.english: One day he was passing by there,
she was sitting and untangling bunches of wool
in the Roman market.
He said to her: Is the distaff pleasing to you,
the one my God gave you?
phrases.notes: He is pointing back to her request in Step 4 that God make her a distaff.

phrases.english: She said to him: Tell your God
to take back what He gave me.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ: אֱלָהָא דִּידַן מֵיהָב יָהֵיב,
phrases.english: He said to her: Our God gives,
but He does not take back.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא חָלֵיף הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the scene from Step 5 by showing the daughter living with the distaff she mockingly asked for.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: God gave the mocker exactly what she asked for, and He does not take it back.

steps.title: What a normal bull looks like, and a donkey is the opposite
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה describes a proper bull: big belly, big hooves, big head, big tail. A donkey is the reverse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says: a bull has a big belly and big hooves, a big head and a big tail. For a donkey it is the opposite.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic, a set of teachings by רב יהודה about bulls. Here he describes the normal body of a bull compared to a donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא spoke about God's greatness. Now it turns to animals. רב יהודה gives a simple description of a good, typical bull, and says a donkey is built the other way.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר כְּרַסְתָּן וּפַרְסְתָן,
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says: A bull has a large belly and large hooves;
its head is large and its tail is large,
phrases.notes: Here רַב just means 'big.' It is not a title like רַב יְהוּדָה.

phrases.english: and the opposite is true for a donkey.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר כְּרַסְתָּן וּפַרְסְתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It moves from the aggadic story to a practical description of animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A typical bull has a big belly, hooves, head and tail. A donkey is the reverse.

steps.title: Why does this description matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference רב יהודה's description makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What practical difference does this make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask why we need to know what a bull looks like. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A description of animal bodies seems like plain nature talk. The גמרא wants to know whether it has any practical use.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: For what purpose is this relevant?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why רב יהודה's description in Step 7 matters.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical use comes from knowing what a normal bull and donkey look like.

steps.title: It matters for buying and selling
steps.stepSummary: The answer: it matters when animals are bought and sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: It matters for buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The description sets the standard for a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone sells a bull, the buyer expects one built like a normal bull. An animal that does not match could be seen as a faulty sale, so the description has a real legal use.

phrases.english: For buying and selling.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The description defines what a buyer can expect when he buys a bull or a donkey.

steps.title: אדם הראשון's bull had one horn
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that the bull אדם הראשון offered had a single horn on its forehead, and brings a פסוק as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה also says: the bull that אדם הראשון offered had one horn on its forehead, as the פסוק says: 'And it shall please God more than a bull with horns and hooves.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives another teaching about a bull, this time the special bull of אדם הראשון. He bases it on a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in תהלים describes the bull with the word מקרין, 'having horns.' רב יהודה reads this word as a hint that the bull had just one horn. The next step will challenge this reading.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר שֶׁהִקְרִיב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן,
phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda says: The bull that Adam the first man sacrificed
had one horn on its forehead,
as it is stated: “And it shall please the Lord more than a bull, a bullock
with horns and hooves.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר שֶׁהִקְרִיב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching by the same רב יהודה about bulls, now about one special bull.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדם הראשון's bull had a single horn, based on the word מקרין.

steps.title: But 'horns' means two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the word מקרין sounds plural, so it should mean two horns, not one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב יהודה's proof. The very word he used seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מקרין is read as a plural form, 'having horns.' So the פסוק looks like it describes a normal bull with two horns, and does not support a one-horned bull at all.

phrases.english: “Makrin” indicates two!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from the פסוק given in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's reading of מקרין as one horn.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word is pronounced as a plural, so it points to two horns.

steps.title: The spelling shows one horn
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that the word is written מקרן, without the extra letter, which hints at one horn.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: it is written מקרן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן defends רב יהודה by looking at how the word is spelled, not how it is read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We read the word as מקרין, which sounds plural. But in the written text it is spelled מקרן, without a י, which looks singular. The spelling is the hint for one horn.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written (the spelling in the text)
The written spelling, without a י, hinting at one horn

steps.confusionAlert: Here the way the word is read aloud and the way it is spelled are different. The גמרא learns from the spelling, even though the reading sounds plural.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said: “Makran” is written.
phrases.notes: The word is read מקרין, but spelled without the י, which looks like 'one horn.'

steps.terutzResolutionType: Learning from the written spelling instead of the pronunciation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the plural reading מקרין means two horns.
steps.terutzMaskana: The written spelling מקרן supports one horn, so רב יהודה's proof holds.

steps.title: The bull's horns came before its hooves
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that the horns of אדם הראשון's bull came before its hooves, since the פסוק says 'horns' before 'hooves.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה also says: the bull אדם הראשון offered had its horns come before its hooves, as the פסוק says: 'with horns and hooves.' Horns are mentioned first, and only then hooves.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a second teaching from the same פסוק, this time learning from the order of the words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says מקרין first and then מפריס. רב יהודה learns from this that the bull's horns appeared first and its hooves after. The common explanation is that this bull was not born from a cow but came up out of the ground head first, so its horns emerged before its hooves.
steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה learns two things about אדם הראשון's bull from one פסוק: from the spelling of מקרין, that it had one horn, and from the order of the words, that its horns came before its hooves.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר שֶׁהִקְרִיב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן,
phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda says: The bull that Adam the first man sacrificed,
its horns came before its hooves,
as it is stated: “And it shall please the Lord more than a bull, a bullock
phrases.notes: תהלים 69:32, the same פסוק as before.

phrases.english: with horns and hooves.”
“With horns” comes first, and then “hooves.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר שֶׁהִקְרִיב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, קַרְנָיו קוֹדְמוֹת לְפַרְסוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching by רב יהודה about the same bull from the same פסוק, now based on word order.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The horns of אדם הראשון's bull came before its hooves, learned from the order of the words in the פסוק.

steps.title: The bull supports the idea that creation was made fully grown
steps.stepSummary: The teaching about אדם הראשון's bull supports רבי יהושע בן לוי, who says all of creation was made fully grown, with full understanding and full form.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רבי יהושע בן לוי. He said: everything in creation was made at its full height, with its full understanding, and in its full form. The פסוק says 'the heavens and earth and all their host (צבאם) were finished.' Don't read it only as 'their host.' Read it as 'their form (צביונם).'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the bull with ready-made horns backs up a bigger teaching of רבי יהושע בן לוי: everything was created fully grown.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bull that came out with grown horns was made as a full adult, not as a baby animal. רבי יהושע בן לוי says this is true of all of creation: full size, full understanding, and full form. He reads צבאם as if it said צביונם to hint at this.

keyTerms.meaning: This supports him; an earlier teaching backs up someone's view
The works of creation; everything made during the six days
At their full height, fully grown
Their form or beauty; the way each creation wanted to look
Do not read it as... (a way of drawing an extra hint from a word)

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not change the words of the תורה. It is a way of drawing an extra hint from how a word sounds.
steps.whyThisMatters: This idea, that creation was made complete, is the background for the next story about the grasses.

phrases.aramaic: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי,
phrases.english: This supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi,
phrases.notes: The bull coming out with full horns shows it was made fully grown, and that is his point.

phrases.english: for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
All the works of creation were created at their full height,
they were created with their full understanding,
they were created in their full form,
as it says: 'And the heavens and the earth and all their host were finished,'
do not read 'their host' but 'their form.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב יהודה's teaching about the horns as support for a wider principle about creation.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching that all of creation was made fully grown, with full understanding and full form.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The bull of אדם הראשון, which came out with horns already grown (step 13).

steps.title: The angel's verse and the grasses' reasoning begins
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפא teaches that the angel in charge of the world said the פסוק 'May the glory of ה׳ be forever.' It happened when the grasses made a קל וחומר after ה׳ told the trees to grow 'after their kind.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר פפא taught about the פסוק 'May the glory of ה׳ be forever; may ה׳ rejoice in His works.' The angel in charge of the world said this פסוק. When ה׳ said 'after its kind' about the trees, the grasses made a קל וחומר about themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אגדה begins. The גמרא tells us who said a פסוק in תהלים and sets up the grasses' reasoning, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At creation, the words 'after its kind' were said about the trees, not clearly about the grasses. The grasses noticed this and drew a lesson for themselves. This fits the idea from the last step that creations were made with understanding.

keyTerms.meaning: The minister of the world; the angel in charge of the world
After its kind; each type separate
A 'how much more so' argument: if it is true for the weaker case, it is surely true for the stronger case

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa expounded:
'May the glory of ה׳ be forever,
may ה׳ rejoice in His works' —
this verse was said by the minister of the world,
phrases.notes: This is the angel put in charge of the world.

phrases.english: At the time that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said
'after its kind' about the trees,
the grasses made a kal vachomer about themselves:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new אגדה that continues the theme of creations having understanding.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק 'May the glory of ה׳ be forever' was said by the angel of the world when the grasses reasoned about themselves.

steps.title: The grasses' two-part reasoning
steps.stepSummary: The grasses reason two ways. First: if ה׳ wanted mixing, why say 'after its kind' about trees? Second: if trees, which don't grow mixed, were told this, then grasses, which do, surely should be.
steps.simpleTranslation: If ה׳ wanted plants to be mixed together, why did He say 'after its kind' about the trees? And here is a קל וחומר too: trees don't usually grow mixed together, and still ה׳ said 'after its kind' about them. We grasses must keep to our kinds all the more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the actual words of the grasses' reasoning that was set up in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first argument says ה׳ clearly cares about keeping kinds apart. The second is the קל וחומר. Trees are big and grow apart, so they are less likely to mix, yet they were told to stay by kind. Grasses grow tangled together, so they need it even more.

keyTerms.meaning: Mixing, a jumble of different kinds together
All the more so; the closing line of a קל וחומר

phrases.aramaic: אִם רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעִרְבּוּבְיָא,
phrases.english: If the will of the Holy One, Blessed be He, were for mixing,
why did He say 'after its kind' about the trees?
And moreover, a kal vachomer:
Now if trees,
which do not usually grow mixed together,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, said 'after its kind' about them,
then for us, all the more so!
phrases.notes: Grasses naturally grow all tangled together, so they need to stay by kind even more.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעִרְבּוּבְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the קל וחומר that step 15 said the grasses made.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The grasses concluded that they too must grow according to their kinds.

steps.title: The grasses grow by kind and the angel praises ה׳
steps.stepSummary: Right away every grass came up by its own kind. The angel of the world then praised ה׳ with the פסוק 'May the glory of ה׳ be forever.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Right away, each and every one came out by its own kind. The angel in charge of the world began and said: 'May the glory of ה׳ be forever; may ה׳ rejoice in His works.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The grasses act on their reasoning, and the angel says the פסוק from the start of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the circle that opened in step 15, explaining when and why the angel said this פסוק. ה׳ can rejoice in His works because the grasses did His will even without being told outright.

keyTerms.meaning: Came out by its own kind
May ה׳ rejoice in His works

steps.whatToRemember: Creations were made complete and with understanding. The grasses showed this by figuring out ה׳'s will on their own, which led the angel to praise ה׳ with 'May the glory of ה׳ be forever.'

phrases.aramaic: מִיָּד כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד יָצָא לְמִינוֹ,
phrases.english: Immediately, each and every one came out by its own kind,
the minister of the world began and said:
'May the glory of ה׳ be forever,
may ה׳ rejoice in His works.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיָּד כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד יָצָא לְמִינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story by showing the result of the grasses' קל וחומר.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The grasses grew by kind on their own, and the angel of the world praised ה׳ with the פסוק from תהלים.

steps.title: רבינא's case: grafting two grasses together
steps.stepSummary: רבינא raises a בעיא about someone who grafts two kinds of grass onto each other. This line only describes the case; the question itself comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא asked: What if a person grafted two kinds of grass onto each other?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new question. רבינא describes a case of grafting two grasses together, and the actual question about it comes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grafting is normally done with trees. רבינא asks about doing it with grasses. This follows right after the גמרא told us that at Creation every grass came up by its own kind (Step 17). So far we only have the case; the question is still to come.

keyTerms.meaning: An open question or dilemma that a sage raises
He grafted, meaning he joined one plant onto another so they grow together
Grasses or small plants, as opposed to trees

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the question or the answer in this line yet. It only describes the case. What רבינא actually wants to know comes in the next line.

phrases.english: Ravina raised a dilemma:

phrases.aramaic: הִרְכִּיב שְׁנֵי דְּשָׁאִים זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה
phrases.english: If one grafted two kinds of grass onto one another,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Right after the story of the grasses coming up by their own kinds (Step 17), the גמרא moves to a new question about grafting grasses together.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the halacha treats a person who grafts two kinds of grass onto each other. The actual question comes in the next line.
